item.research_question: How do stacking fault energy, shear modulus, and lattice distortion influence the Hall–Petch coefficient and grain growth kinetics in FCC-structured high/medium entropy alloys?
item.material_system: Equiatomic FeCoNiCrPd, FeCoNiCrMn, and their quaternary (FeCoNiCr, FeCoNiMn) and ternary (CoNiCr, CoNiMn) derivatives
item.processing_route: Vacuum arc melting (6 remelts), homogenization at 1100–1200 °C for 24 h, 80% cold rolling at room temperature, annealing at 800–1200 °C for 1–4 h, water quenching
item.test_conditions: Annealing temperatures 800–1200 °C; annealing times 1–4 h; Vickers microhardness (500 gf load, 15 s); grain size via linear intercept method (ASTM E112-12)
key_findings: All H/MEAs follow the Hall–Petch equation H = H0 + KH·d^(-1/2) after annealing at 800–1200 °C for 1 h.
The FeCoNiCrPd alloy exhibits the highest hardness at a given grain size due to the largest Young's modulus difference between Cr and Pd (130.5%).
The Hall–Petch coefficient (KH) is mainly dominated by the alloy's stacking fault energy and shear modulus, not lattice distortion (δ).
The grain growth exponent (n) for all alloys is less than 0.5, attributed to solute drag effects.
The activation energy for grain growth (QG) for FeCoNiCrPd is 831.9 kJ/mol, significantly higher than other H/MEAs (300–500 kJ/mol).
QG values for all H/MEAs are much higher than those of conventional alloys (e.g., stainless steel, Mg, Ti alloys).
Substitution of Mn for Cr lowers the shear modulus and decreases the KH value (e.g., FeCoNiCr: 84 GPa → FeCoNiMn: 77 GPa).
Higher diffusion coefficients (D) correlate with lower QG values; Mn addition lowers QG due to its high diffusion rate.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that KH is controlled by the combination of stacking fault energy and shear modulus, where high SFE and low shear modulus reduce KH. Hardness at a fixed grain size is driven by Young's modulus misfit. Grain growth kinetics are diffusion-controlled; high lattice distortion in H/MEAs hinders atomic diffusion and grain boundary migration, leading to high QG values. Mn lowers QG because it has the highest diffusion rate among constituent elements.
item.limitations: The text notes that the δ value order is hardly correlated to KH values, suggesting other factors may be at play. The authors also state that the solute drag effect in equiatomic H/MEAs is difficult to quantify due to the absence of a sole principal element and requires further investigation. Additionally, discrepancies in KH and QG values compared to other studies are attributed to differences in pre-treatments (homogenization, cold-rolling reduction, annealing temperature).
item.future_work: The authors suggest that the solute drag effect in equiatomic H/MEAs needs further investigations. They also propose that the deviation in KH values for FeCoNiCrMn may be caused by high grain size deviation and requires further study. The causes of differences in QG and KH values between studies are suggested to be deviations in composition, impurities, annealing temperatures, and cold-rolling amounts.
quotes: The Hall–Petch coefficient KH value being mainly dominated by the alloy's stacking fault energy and shear modulus.
The FeCoNiCrPd alloy exhibits the highest hardness of the H/MEAs at the same grain size due to the largest Young's modulus difference between Cr and Pd.

The results demonstrate that the QG values of these H/MEAs are much higher than those of conventional alloys; most notable is FeCoNiCrPd HEA, which has an unusually lattice distortion effect that hinders grain growth.
